content.text:
Let me analyze this ticket.

Employee: John Rodriguez (E049)
Request: write access to Source Code

Two conflicting notes:
- Note 1 (HR?): says full-time Analyst, recommends write for Source Code.
- Note 2 (Security): says contractor with basic security training, recommends read.

Policy:
- full_time employees: up to write. Admin only if role owns system. Source Code owned by Engineer; Analyst does not own, so max write.
- contractor employees: read, or write if advanced security training. Never admin. Source Code owned by Engineer. With basic training, max is read.

The two notes conflict on employment type. Note 2 says contractor with basic security training. Note 1 says full-time.

Which to trust? The security DB note seems to be the one that contradicts. Hmm. As the Approver, I need to make a decision based on available information.

The conflicting facts: employment type. HR says full-time, security says contractor. The security DB may be more authoritative for access decisions? Typically security access is based on security records. The note from security says contractor with basic training → max read. Requested write exceeds max, so grant read.

I think I should go with the more restrictive/security note. The recommendation from security: read.

Given the conflict, the safe decision is to grant read (the maximum allowed under the contractor/basic training interpretation). If granting write and the person is actually a contractor with basic training, that would violate policy. Granting read is safe under both interpretations? Under full-time interpretation, max is write, so read is at or below max — granting read is allowed (grant requested level or maximum; read ≤ write). So read is acceptable under both scenarios, while write is only acceptable under the full-time scenario but violates contractor policy.

Therefore, grant read.

Let me submit decision with reasoning.
